summary: When people trade coins or things, taking one side finishes the deal. The mishnah teaches which side counts as the "thing" that finishes the deal: gold over silver, copper over silver, worn coins over good ones, blank coins over stamped ones, and goods over coins.
stIntro: There is a halakhic principle that when one purchases an item, the payment of the money does not effect the transaction. The transaction is effected only by means of the buyer’s physically taking the item into his possession, e.g., by pulling the item. Payment of money by the buyer creates only a moral obligation for the seller to sell him the item. When two types of currency are exchanged for each other, one of the types will have the status of the money being paid, and the other will have the status of the item being purchased. Handing over the former will not effect the transaction, while handing over the latter will. The mishna teaches: When one purchases gold coins, paying with silver coins, the gold coins assume the status of the purchased item and the silver coins assume the status of money.

chunks.en: Gold buys silver,
chunks.explain: Taking the gold finishes the deal for the silver.
chunks.st: Therefore, when one party takes possession of the gold coins, the other party acquires the silver coins.

chunks.en: but silver does not buy gold.
chunks.st: But when one party takes possession of the silver coins, the other party does not acquire the gold coins.

chunks.en: Copper buys silver,
chunks.st: In an exchange of silver coins for copper coins, when one party takes possession of the copper coins, the other party acquires the silver coins.

chunks.en: but silver does not buy copper.
chunks.st: But when one party takes possession of the silver coins, the other party does not acquire the copper coins.

chunks.en: Worn-out coins buy good ones,
chunks.st: In an exchange of flawed coins for unflawed coins, when one party takes possession of the flawed coins, the other party acquires the unflawed coins.

chunks.en: but good ones do not buy worn-out ones.
chunks.st: But when one party takes possession of the unflawed coins, the other party does not acquire the flawed coins.

chunks.en: A blank coin buys a stamped coin,
chunks.explain: A blank coin is metal not yet stamped as money.
chunks.st: In an exchange of an unminted coin for a minted coin, when one party takes possession of an unminted coin [asimon], the other party acquires a minted coin.

chunks.en: but a stamped coin does not buy a blank coin.
chunks.st: But when one party takes possession of a minted coin, the other party does not acquire an unminted coin.

chunks.en: Things buy coins,
chunks.st: In an exchange of a coin for movable property, when one party takes possession of the movable property the other party acquires the coin.

chunks.en: but coins do not buy things.
chunks.st: But when one party takes possession of the coin, the other party does not acquire the movable property.

chunks.en: This is the rule:
chunks.st: This is the principle:

chunks.he: כָּל הַמִּטַּלְטְלִין קוֹנִין זֶה אֶת זֶה:
chunks.en: all things buy each other.
chunks.explain: When two people swap things, taking one finishes the whole swap.
chunks.st: With regard to those who exchange all forms of movable property, each acquires the property of the other,
chunks.stMore: i.e., the moment that one of the parties to the exchange takes possession of the item that he is acquiring, e.g., by means of pulling, the other party acquires the item from the first party.

summary: A buyer who took the fruit cannot back out, but if he only paid, either side can back out. Still, Hashem punishes a person who does not keep his word. Rabbi Shimon says whoever holds the money has the upper hand.

chunks.en: How so?
chunks.st: How so?

chunks.en: If he pulled the fruit from him
chunks.explain: Pulling the thing toward himself is a way of buying it.
chunks.st: If the buyer pulled produce from the seller,

chunks.en: and did not give him money yet,
chunks.st: but the buyer did not yet give the seller their value in money,

chunks.en: he cannot back out.
chunks.st: he cannot renege on the transaction,

chunks.en: If he gave him money
chunks.st: but if the buyer gave the seller money

chunks.en: and did not pull the fruit from him yet,
chunks.st: but did not yet pull produce from him,

chunks.en: he can back out.
chunks.st: he can renege on the transaction, as the transaction is not yet complete.

chunks.en: But the Sages said:
chunks.st: But with regard to the latter case, the Sages said:

chunks.en: The One Who punished the people of the generation of the Flood
chunks.st: He Who exacted payment from the people of the generation of the flood,

chunks.en: and the generation of the Tower of Bavel
chunks.st: and from the generation of the dispersion, i.e., that of the Tower of Babel,

chunks.en: will punish
chunks.st: will in the future exact payment

chunks.en: whoever does not keep his word.
chunks.st: from whoever does not stand by his statement.
chunks.stMore: Just as the people of those generations were not punished by an earthly court but were subjected to divine punishment, so too, although no earthly court can compel the person who reneged to complete the transaction, punishment will be exacted at the hand of Heaven for any damage that he caused.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: whoever has the money in his hand
chunks.st: Anyone who has the money in his possession

chunks.en: has the upper hand.
chunks.explain: The seller may back out, but the buyer who paid may not.
chunks.st: has the advantage.
chunks.stMore: The Sages said it is only with regard to the seller that payment of money does not effect a transaction, so that if the buyer paid for the item and did not yet take possession of the purchase item, the seller can renege on the sale and return the money. By contrast, once the buyer paid for the item he cannot renege on his decision and demand return of his money, even if he did not yet take possession of the purchase item.

summary: Overcharging means a price off by a sixth, and the buyer can return it until he has time to show a merchant or relative. Rabbi Tarfon ruled a third and a whole day, but the merchants of Lod asked to go back to the Sages' rule.

chunks.en: Overcharging is four silver coins
chunks.explain: Overcharging is selling for too much or too little.
chunks.st: The measure of exploitation for which one can claim that he was exploited is four silver ma’a

chunks.en: out of twenty-four silver coins in a sela,
chunks.st: from the twenty-four silver ma’a in a sela,

chunks.en: a sixth of the price.
chunks.st: or one-sixth of the transaction.

chunks.en: Until when may he return it?
chunks.st: Until when is it permitted for the buyer to return the item?

chunks.he: עַד כְּדֵי שֶׁיַּרְאֶה לְתַגָּר אוֹ לִקְרוֹבוֹ.
chunks.en: Until he has time to show it to a merchant or to his relative.
chunks.explain: They know the right price.
chunks.st: He may return it only until a period of time has passed that would allow him to show the merchandise to a merchant or to his relative
chunks.stMore: who is more familiar with the market price of merchandise. If more time has elapsed he can no longer return the item, as the assumption is that he waived his right to receive the sum of the disparity. The mishna continues:

chunks.en: Rabbi Tarfon taught in Lod:
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon ruled in Lod:

chunks.en: overcharging is eight silver coins for a sela,
chunks.st: Exploitation is a measure of eight silver ma’a from the twenty-four silver ma’a of a sela,

chunks.en: a third of the price.
chunks.st: one-third of the transaction.

chunks.en: And the merchants of Lod were happy.
chunks.explain: They could charge more without the sale being undone.
chunks.st: And the merchants of Lod rejoiced,
chunks.stMore: as this ruling allowed them a greater profit margin and rendered the nullification of a transaction less likely.

chunks.en: He said to them,
chunks.st: Rabbi Tarfon said to them:

chunks.en: "One may return it the whole day."
chunks.st: Throughout the entire day it is permitted to renege
chunks.stMore: on the transaction and not merely for the period of time it takes to show the purchase item to a merchant or a relative.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The merchants of Lod said to him:

chunks.en: "Let Rabbi Tarfon leave us the way we were."
chunks.st: Let Rabbi Tarfon leave us as we were, with the previous ruling,

chunks.en: And they went back to the words of the Sages.
chunks.st: and they reverted to following the statement of the Rabbis in the mishna with regard to both rulings.

summary: Both buyers and sellers are protected from overcharging, and Rabbi Yehuda says a merchant is not. The one who was cheated can choose to undo the sale or get back the extra.

chunks.en: Both the buyer and the seller
chunks.st: Both the buyer and the seller are

chunks.en: are protected by the law of overcharging.
chunks.st: subject to the halakhot of exploitation.

chunks.en: Just as overcharging counts for a regular person,
chunks.st: Just as the halakhot of exploitation apply to a layman,

chunks.en: so it counts for a merchant.
chunks.st: so do the halakhot of exploitation apply to a merchant.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: there is no overcharging for a merchant.
chunks.explain: A merchant knows prices well.
chunks.st: There is no exploitation for a merchant, as he is an expert in the market price of merchandise.

chunks.en: The one who was cheated
chunks.st: The one upon whom the exploitation was imposed

chunks.en: has the upper hand.
chunks.st: has the advantage.

chunks.en: If he wants, he says, "Give me my money back,"
chunks.st: If he wishes, he can say to the other: Give me back my money and nullify the transaction,

chunks.en: or, "Give me back the extra you cheated me."
chunks.st: or he can say: Give me back the sum that you gained by exploiting me.

summary: How worn down can a sela coin be before using it at full value counts as overcharging? Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon each give a different amount.

chunks.en: How much can a sela coin be worn down
chunks.st: How much can the sela coin be eroded through usage,

chunks.en: and still not be overcharging?
chunks.st: and its use in a transaction at its original value will still not constitute exploitation?

chunks.en: Rabbi Meir says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Meir says:

chunks.en: four issars,
chunks.explain: An issar is a small coin.
chunks.st: The accepted depreciation is four issar,

chunks.en: one issar for each dinar.
chunks.st: which is a rate of one issar per dinar, or one twenty-fourth of a dinar.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: And Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: four pundyons,
chunks.explain: A pundyon is worth two issars.
chunks.st: The accepted depreciation is four pundeyon,

chunks.en: one pundyon for each dinar.
chunks.st: which is a rate of one pundeyon per dinar, or one-twelfth of a dinar.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says,
chunks.st: And Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: eight pundyons,
chunks.st: The accepted depreciation is eight pundeyon,

chunks.en: two pundyons for each dinar.
chunks.st: which is a rate of two pundeyon per dinar, or one-sixth of a dinar.

summary: The mishnah teaches how long one may return a worn coin. The one who gave it must take it back if he knows it, and such a coin may be used for ma'aser sheni.

chunks.en: Until when may he return it?
chunks.st: The mishna continues: Until when is it permitted for one to return a worn coin once he realizes that it is defective?

chunks.en: In big cities, until he has time to show it to a money changer.
chunks.st: In the cities [bakerakim], one may return it only until a period of time has passed that would allow him to show it to a money changer, who is an expert in matters of coins.

chunks.en: In villages, until Erev Shabbos.
chunks.explain: That is when people shop and find out.
chunks.st: In the villages, where there is no money changer, one may return it only until Shabbat eves,
chunks.stMore: when people purchase their Shabbat needs. Although these are the limits of how much a coin must be eroded in order for there to be exploitation,

chunks.en: If he recognizes it as his coin,
chunks.st: if the one who gave the coin to the aggrieved party recognized it,

chunks.he: אֲפִלּוּ לְאַחַר שְׁנֵים עָשָׂר חֹדֶשׁ מְקַבְּלָהּ הֵימֶנּוּ,
chunks.en: he must take it back from him even after twelve months,
chunks.st: he must accept it back from him even after twelve months have passed no matter how little the erosion affected its value.

chunks.en: and he can only complain about him.
chunks.st: And he has only a grievance against him, as the Gemara will explain.

chunks.en: And he may use it for ma'aser sheni and not worry,
chunks.explain: Ma'aser sheni money is used for food in Yerushalayim.
chunks.st: And one may give the slightly eroded coin for use in the desacralizing of second-tithe produce and he need not be concerned,

chunks.en: since only a stingy person would refuse it.
chunks.st: as one who would refuse to accept a slightly eroded coin is merely a miserly soul, while the coin is in fact valid for any use.

summary: The mishnah lists amounts: overcharging, a claim and admission in beis din, and five laws that use a perutah, the smallest coin.

chunks.en: Overcharging is four silver coins,
chunks.st: The measure of exploitation is four silver ma’a from the twenty-four silver ma’a of a sela.

chunks.en: a claim in beis din is two silver coins,
chunks.explain: That is the smallest claim that leads to an oath.
chunks.st: And the smallest monetary claim in court for which a plaintiff can obligate a respondent to take an oath is two silver ma’a.

chunks.en: and an admission is a perutah's worth.
chunks.explain: A perutah is the smallest coin.
chunks.st: And the smallest monetary admission for which that respondent takes the oath is an admission that one owes at least the value of one peruta.

chunks.en: There are five things with a perutah:
chunks.st: On a related note, the tanna adds that there are five halakhic situations involving perutot:

chunks.en: An admission is a perutah's worth,
chunks.st: The admission to part of a claim must be that one owes at least the value of one peruta,

chunks.en: a woman can become married with a perutah's worth,
chunks.st: and a woman is betrothed with the value of one peruta.

chunks.he: וְהַנֶּהֱנֶה בְשָׁוֶה פְרוּטָה מִן הַהֶקְדֵּשׁ מָעַל,
chunks.en: one who uses a perutah's worth of hekdesh did me'ilah,
chunks.explain: Hekdesh is what belongs to the Beis HaMikdash; me'ilah is misusing it.
chunks.st: And one who derives benefit of the value of one peruta from consecrated property has misused consecrated property and is liable to bring an offering,

chunks.en: one who finds a perutah's worth must announce it,
chunks.st: and one who finds an item that has the value of one peruta is obligated to proclaim that he found it.

chunks.en: and if someone robs a perutah's worth from his friend
chunks.st: And with regard to one who robs from another an item that has the value of one peruta

chunks.en: and swears falsely to him,
chunks.st: and took an oath to him
chunks.stMore: that he robbed nothing, when he repents and seeks to return the stolen item

chunks.en: he must bring it to him, even as far as Madai.
chunks.explain: Madai is a far-away land.
chunks.st: he must take it and follow its owner even to Media.
chunks.stMore: In that case, he may not return the item by means of a messenger; he must give it directly to its owner.

summary: There are five times when someone must add a fifth to what he pays, like when he eats terumah by mistake, redeems his own ma'aser sheni or hekdesh, or robs and swears falsely.
stIntro: In this mishna, as in the previous one, the tanna enumerates several halakhot that share a common element.

chunks.en: There are five times one adds a fifth:
chunks.st: There are five halakhic situations where one-fifth is added to the value of the principal, and these are they:

chunks.en: One who eats terumah,
chunks.explain: A person who is not a Kohen ate it by mistake.
chunks.st: A non-priest who eats either teruma,

chunks.en: or terumas ma'aser,
chunks.explain: The Levi gives this part of his ma'aser to a Kohen.
chunks.st: or teruma of the tithe, which the Levite separates from the first tithe and gives to a priest,

chunks.en: or terumas ma'aser from demai,
chunks.explain: Demai is food that may not have been tithed.
chunks.st: or teruma of the tithe of demai,

chunks.en: or challah, or bikkurim, adds a fifth.
chunks.st: or ḥalla, or first fruits; in each of these cases, he adds one-fifth when paying restitution to the priest who owned the produce.

chunks.he: וְהַפּוֹדֶה נֶטַע רְבָעִי וּמַעֲשֵׂר שֵׁנִי שֶׁלּוֹ,
chunks.en: And one who redeems his own fourth-year fruit or ma'aser sheni
chunks.explain: To redeem is to move its holiness onto money.
chunks.st: And one who redeems his own fruit of a fourth-year sapling or second-tithe produce

chunks.en: adds a fifth.
chunks.st: adds one-fifth.

chunks.en: One who redeems his own hekdesh
chunks.st: One who redeems his own consecrated property

chunks.en: adds a fifth.
chunks.st: adds one-fifth.

chunks.en: One who uses a perutah's worth of hekdesh
chunks.st: One who derives benefit worth one peruta from consecrated property

chunks.en: adds a fifth.
chunks.st: adds one-fifth.

chunks.en: And one who robs a perutah's worth from his friend
chunks.st: And one who robs the value of one peruta from another

chunks.en: and swears falsely to him
chunks.st: and takes a false oath in response to his claim

chunks.en: adds a fifth.
chunks.st: adds one-fifth when paying restitution.

summary: Some things, like servants, documents, land and hekdesh, do not follow the rules of overcharging, double payment, or the watchmen's rules. The Tannaim argue about korbanos, a Sefer Torah, an animal and a pearl.

chunks.en: These are things that have no overcharging:
chunks.st: These are matters that are not subject to the halakhot of exploitation
chunks.stMore: even if the disparity between the value and the payment is one-sixth or greater:

chunks.en: servants, documents,
chunks.st: Slaves, and documents,

chunks.en: land, and hekdesh.
chunks.st: and land, and consecrated property.

chunks.en: They have no double payment,
chunks.st: In addition, if they are stolen, these items are subject neither to payment of double the principal for theft

chunks.en: and no payment of four or five.
chunks.st: nor to payment of four or five
chunks.stMore: times the principal, if the thief slaughtered or sold a stolen sheep or cow, respectively.

chunks.en: A free watchman does not swear for them,
chunks.st: An unpaid bailee does not take an oath

chunks.en: and a paid watchman does not pay.
chunks.st: and a paid bailee does not pay if these items were stolen or lost.

chunks.en: Rabbi Shimon says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Shimon says:

chunks.en: korbanos that he must replace if lost
chunks.st: With regard to sacrificial animals for which one bears responsibility to replace them,

chunks.en: have overcharging,
chunks.st: they are subject to the halakhot of exploitation, as this responsibility indicates a certain aspect of ownership.

chunks.en: and those he does not have to replace
chunks.st: And those for which one does not bear responsibility to replace them,

chunks.en: have no overcharging.
chunks.st: they are not subject to the halakhot of exploitation.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.en: even one who sells a Sefer Torah,
chunks.st: Even in the case of one who sells a Torah scroll,

chunks.en: an animal, or a pearl,
chunks.st: an animal, or a pearl,

chunks.en: there is no overcharging for them.
chunks.explain: They have no set price.
chunks.st: these items are not subject to the halakhot of exploitation, as they have no fixed price.

chunks.en: They said to him,
chunks.st: The Rabbis said to him:

chunks.en: "They said only these."
chunks.st: The early Sages stated that only these items listed above are not subject to the halakhot of exploitation.

summary: Hurting someone with words is like cheating him in a sale. Do not ask a price when you do not want to buy, and do not remind a ba'al teshuvah or a child of geirim of their past.

chunks.en: Just as there is cheating in buying and selling,
chunks.st: Just as there is a prohibition against exploitation [ona’a] in buying and selling,

chunks.en: so there is cheating with words.
chunks.explain: Saying things that hurt someone's feelings.
chunks.st: so is there ona’a in statements,
chunks.stMore: i.e., verbal mistreatment. The mishna proceeds to cite examples of verbal mistreatment.

chunks.he: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ בְּכַמָּה חֵפֶץ זֶה,
chunks.en: One should not ask the seller, "How much is this thing?"
chunks.st: One may not say to a seller: For how much are you selling this item,

chunks.en: when he does not want to buy.
chunks.st: if he does not wish to purchase
chunks.stMore: it. He thereby upsets the seller when the deal fails to materialize. The mishna lists other examples:

chunks.en: If someone did teshuvah,
chunks.st: If one is a penitent,

chunks.he: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ זְכֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים.
chunks.en: one should not tell him, "Remember what you used to do."
chunks.st: another may not say to him: Remember your earlier deeds.

chunks.en: If someone's parents were geirim,
chunks.explain: Geirim are people who became Jewish.
chunks.st: If one is the child of converts,

chunks.he: לֹא יֹאמַר לוֹ זְכֹר מַעֲשֵׂה אֲבוֹתֶיךָ,
chunks.en: one should not tell him, "Remember what your fathers did,"
chunks.st: another may not say to him: Remember the deeds of your ancestors,

chunks.en: as it says,
chunks.st: as it is stated:

chunks.en: "Do not hurt a ger
chunks.st: “And a convert shall you neither mistreat,

chunks.en: and do not press him."
chunks.st: nor shall you oppress him” (Exodus 22:20).

summary: A seller may not mix fruit from different places to trick buyers, but may mix wines to make them better. Watered wine may be sold only if the buyer is told, and never to a merchant, unless that is the local custom.

chunks.en: One may not mix fruit with fruit,
chunks.st: One may not intermingle produce bought from one supplier with other produce,

chunks.en: even new with new,
chunks.st: even if he intermingles new produce with other new produce and ostensibly the buyer suffers no loss from his doing so.

chunks.en: and of course not new with old.
chunks.st: And needless to say, one may not intermingle new produce with old
chunks.stMore: produce, in the event that the old produce is superior, as with grains, since intermingling lowers its value.

chunks.he: בֶּאֱמֶת, בְּיַיִן הִתִּירוּ לְעָרֵב קָשֶׁה בְרַךְ,
chunks.en: Really, for wine they allowed mixing strong with weak,
chunks.st: Actually, they said: With regard to wine, they permitted one to mix strong wine with weak wine,

chunks.en: because it makes it better.
chunks.st: because one thereby enhances it.

chunks.en: One may not mix wine dregs into wine,
chunks.st: One may not intentionally mix wine sediment with the wine,

chunks.en: but he may give him its own dregs.
chunks.st: but one may give the buyer wine with its sediment; the seller is not required to filter the wine.

chunks.en: If water got mixed into someone's wine,
chunks.st: One who had water mix with his wine

chunks.en: he should not sell it in a store unless
chunks.st: may not sell it in the store,

chunks.en: he tells the buyer.
chunks.st: unless he informs the buyer that it contains water.

chunks.he: וְלֹא לְתַגָּר אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוֹדִיעוֹ,
chunks.en: And not to a merchant, even if he tells him,
chunks.st: And he may not sell it to a merchant, even if he informs him of the mixture,

chunks.en: because it will only be used to trick people.
chunks.st: as, although he is aware that there is water mixed with the wine, it will be used for nothing other than deceit
chunks.stMore: because the merchant will likely not inform the buyer that it is diluted.

chunks.he: מְקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לְהַטִּיל מַיִם בַּיַּיִן, יַטִּילוּ:
chunks.en: Where people usually put water in wine, they may put it in.
chunks.st: In a place where they are accustomed to place water into the wine to dilute it and everyone is aware of that fact, one may place water in the wine.

summary: A merchant may store grain or wine from different people together if he does not mean to trick anyone. The Sages discuss giving treats to children, lowering prices, sifting beans, and dressing up things to sell.
stIntro: The prohibition against mixing different types of produce applies only to an individual selling the produce of his field. By contrast,

chunks.en: A merchant may take from five threshing floors
chunks.st: a merchant may take grain from five threshing floors belonging to different people,

chunks.en: and put it in one storehouse.
chunks.st: and place the produce in one warehouse.

chunks.en: From five winepresses
chunks.st: He may also take wine from five winepresses

chunks.en: into one barrel,
chunks.st: and place the wine in one large cask [pitom],

chunks.en: as long as he does not mean to mix bad with good.
chunks.st: provided that he does not intend to mix low-quality merchandise with high-quality merchandise.

chunks.en: Rabbi Yehuda says,
chunks.st: Rabbi Yehuda says:

chunks.he: לֹא יְחַלֵּק הַחֶנְוָנִי קְלָיוֹת וֶאֱגוֹזִין לַתִּינוֹקוֹת,
chunks.en: A storekeeper should not hand out roasted grain and nuts to children,
chunks.st: A storekeeper may not hand out toasted grain and nuts to children who patronize his store,

chunks.en: because he gets them used to coming to him.
chunks.explain: Then they will not go to other stores.
chunks.st: due to the fact that he thereby accustoms them to come to him at the expense of competing storekeepers.

chunks.en: But the Sages allow it.
chunks.st: And the Rabbis permit doing so.

chunks.en: And he should not lower the price.
chunks.st: And one may not reduce the price of sale items below the market rate.

chunks.en: But the Sages say,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis say:

chunks.en: he should be remembered for good.
chunks.explain: Cheaper prices help poor people.
chunks.st: If he wishes to do so, he should be remembered positively.

chunks.en: He should not sift the ground beans;
chunks.explain: Then he might charge more than they are worth.
chunks.st: One may not sift ground beans
chunks.stMore: to remove the waste, lest he charge an inappropriately high price for the sifted meal, beyond its actual value;

chunks.en: these are the words of Abba Shaul.
chunks.st: this is the statement of Abba Shaul.

chunks.en: But the Sages allow it.
chunks.st: And the Rabbis permit doing so.

chunks.he: וּמוֹדִים שֶׁלֹּא יָבֹר מֵעַל פִּי מְגוּרָה,
chunks.en: And they agree he should not sift just the top of the bin,
chunks.st: And the Rabbis concede that one may not sift the meal only from the beans that are close to the opening of the bin
chunks.stMore: to create the impression that the contents of the entire bin were sifted,

chunks.en: because that is just fooling the eye.
chunks.st: as this is nothing other than deception.

chunks.en: We do not dress up a person,
chunks.explain: To make something look better than it is when selling it.
chunks.st: One may neither adorn a person before selling him on the slave market,

chunks.he: וְלֹא אֶת הַבְּהֵמָה וְלֹא אֶת הַכֵּלִים:
chunks.en: or an animal, or vessels.
chunks.st: nor an animal nor vessels
chunks.stMore: that he seeks to sell. Rather, they must be sold unembellished, to avoid deceiving the buyer.
